Conversation, family & daily routines

after all adverb

also in the end, after all (you must remember), of course

classical

Lucr. 5.137: soleret tandem in eōdem homine manēre, in the end, after all (Lewis & Short s.v. tandem)
Ter. And. 3.4.7: tandem cognōstī quī siem (Lewis & Short)

tandem

in the end, after all

After long delay or against expectation: at last, in the end (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • nempe — of course, surely: after all (giving a reason no one can deny)

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 3.49: nempe eam dīcit, in quā virtūtis nūlla pars īnsit (Lewis & Short s.v. nempe); Traupman 298

    Lewis & Short: “in stating a notorious or obvious fact or truth, certainly, of course”. Where English “after all” reminds the hearer of a reason, Latin often says enim in the second place of the clause.

  • rē vērā — in fact, as it turned out: “after all” against what was expected

    also used · classical · Traupman 92, 269

    Rē vērā is “in fact, in reality”, the fact set against words or appearances (Lewis & Short s.v. rēs; see actually). It fits “after all” only where the English means “as it turned out” (it was not so bad after all); it does not concede or remind, as nempe and enim do.

See also actually, certainly.

SourcesLewis & Short: tandem · Lewis & Short: nempe · Lewis & Short: enim

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 92, 269, 298.
